Stated Claim / Post Context:
Girls’ health improves worldwide, gene therapy partly restores sight, sushi chef helps Somali pirates turn to fishing

In today's edition: a new global index finds girls' health improving in 178 countries, gene therapy research shows promise in restoring some sight in blind people, and a Japanese sushi chef is supporting former Somali pirates find a new livelihood through fishing.

Actual Article Body:
Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on October 14, 2026 |

Photo: Vaishnavi Pawar/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: a new global index finds girls’ health improving in 178 countries, gene therapy research shows promise in restoring some sight in blind people, and a Japanese sushi chef is supporting former Somali pirates find a new livelihood through fishing.

Girls’ health outcomes improved in 178 of 192 countries between 2000 and 2023, according to the first-ever Global Girls’ Index, developed by Plan International Germany and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum. The study assesses health outcomes among more than 971 million girls and young women aged 5 to 19 worldwide.

Source: Squirrel News

The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, uses the same technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light which scooped the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine. It was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021. Now researchers have reported the results from a larger trial involving the original patient and a further nine people.

Source: The Guardian

Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children. Chemotherapy can permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm, leaving children who undergo it at risk of infertility in adulthood.

Source: The Guardian

The FDA has approved the first drug specifically designed to treat Alexander disease, an extremely rare neurological disorder that progressively damages the nervous system and can be fatal. Known as Zanvastro, the treatment is a significant step forward for patients who have long lacked disease-targeting therapies, relying instead on treatments to manage symptoms and complications.

Source: Science Daily

Hungary’s parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, removing provisions that have been used to stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ+ and human rights activists have welcomed the decision while urging lawmakers to repeal other discriminatory laws introduced under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Source: BBC News

Respyre has developed Mosscrete: a bioreceptive concrete designed to support moss growth on vertical surfaces. The material is applied to existing surfaces, allowing a layer of moss to gradually develop. Unlike most plants, moss has no true roots. Instead, it attaches itself using tiny thread-like structures called rhizoids, which do not penetrate or damage the concrete.

Source: Pragmatika

Turning unused lots into fruit orchards where anyone can pick the produce for free means that Giving Grove is creating benefits that extend far beyond fresh food. Today, more than a million people live within walking distance of one of its orchards, and the concept is spreading across the country.

Source: KCUR

The installation of eight canopy bridges in Alta Floresta has enabled 15,000 safe crossings by animals including spider monkeys and marmosets – and more bridges are planned elsewhere. The bridges are part of a programme involving Projeto Reconecta and the municipal government, along with local organisations and business owners.

Source: The Guardian

As Palestinians displaced by Israel’s war in Gaza begin rebuilding their lives in Mexico City, a growing number are turning to food to support their families and preserve their cultural traditions. Though their numbers remain small, these newcomers are establishing businesses and introducing locals to Palestinian cuisine, all while finding ways to reconnect with their homeland.

Source: Arab News

A Japanese sushi entrepreneur took an unconventional approach to one of the world’s most persistent piracy crises. By helping former Somali pirates find opportunities in fishing, Kiyoshi Kimura, CEO of the popular Japanese sushi chain Sushizanmai, offered an alternative to a life at sea marked by hijackings and violence.

Source: Japan Daily
